solution:
Werner explained bonding in coordination compounds through four postulates.

1. In coordination compounds a metal shows two kinds of linkage or valence — a primary valence and a secondary valence.

2. The primary valence is ionisable and is satisfied by negative ions. It corresponds to the oxidation number of the metal.

3. The secondary valence is non-ionisable and is satisfied by neutral molecules or by negative ions. It corresponds to the coordination number and is fixed for a given metal.

4. The groups bound by the secondary valence occupy fixed positions in space, so every coordination number has its own characteristic geometry — coordination number 6 gives an octahedral arrangement, coordination number 4 gives either a tetrahedral or a square planar arrangement.

In a formula the primary valences are shown by broken lines and the secondary valences by full lines. For example in \(\text{CoCl}_3\cdot 6\text{NH}_3\), written as \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]\text{Cl}_3\), cobalt has a primary valence of 3 satisfied by the three chloride ions outside the sphere, and a secondary valence of 6 satisfied by the six ammonia molecules held octahedrally inside it. Only the three chlorides are ionisable, which is why all three are precipitated by silver nitrate.

The difference is that one mixture gives a double salt and the other gives a complex.

\(\text{FeSO}_4\) and \((\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4\) in a 1:1 molar ratio give Mohr's salt, \(\text{FeSO}_4\cdot(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4\cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}\), which is a **double salt**. A double salt exists only in the solid state; on dissolution it dissociates completely into its constituent simple ions:

\(\text{FeSO}_4\cdot(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{2+} + 2\text{NH}_4^{+} + 2\text{SO}_4^{2-}\)

Free \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) is therefore present in solution and gives the usual test for ferrous ion.

\(\text{CuSO}_4\) and aqueous ammonia in a 1:4 molar ratio give the **coordination compound** \([\text{Cu}(\text{NH}_3)_4]\text{SO}_4\). Here the four ammonia molecules are held inside the coordination sphere, and the complex ion retains its identity in solution:

\([\text{Cu}(\text{NH}_3)_4]\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow [\text{Cu}(\text{NH}_3)_4]^{2+} + \text{SO}_4^{2-}\)

The \([\text{Cu}(\text{NH}_3)_4]^{2+}\) ion has a very high stability constant and dissociates into \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) and \(\text{NH}_3\) only to a negligible extent, so the concentration of free \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) is far too small to answer the test for cupric ion.

**Coordination entity** — a central metal atom or ion bonded to a fixed number of ions or molecules. Examples: \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{3+}\) and \([\text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4]\).

**Ligand** — the ion or molecule bound to the central atom through a donor atom that supplies a lone pair. Examples: \(\text{Cl}^{-}\) and \(\text{NH}_3\).

**Coordination number** — the number of ligand donor atoms directly bonded to the central metal. Examples: 6 in \([\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]^{3-}\) and 4 in \([\text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4]\). Note that for a didentate ligand each donor atom is counted, so it is 6 in \([\text{Co}(\text{en})_3]^{3+}\) although only three ligands are attached.

**Coordination polyhedron** — the spatial arrangement of the ligand donor atoms about the central metal. Examples: octahedral in \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{3+}\) and tetrahedral in \([\text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4]\).

**Homoleptic** — a complex in which the metal is bound to only one kind of donor group. Examples: \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{3+}\) and \([\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]^{3-}\).

**Heteroleptic** — a complex in which the metal is bound to more than one kind of donor group. Examples: \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_4\text{Cl}_2]^{+}\) and \([\text{Pt}(\text{NH}_3)_2\text{Cl}_2]\).

The classification is by the number of donor atoms through which the ligand actually attaches itself to the metal.

**Unidentate** — the ligand binds through a single donor atom. Examples: \(\text{Cl}^{-}\) and \(\text{NH}_3\).

**Didentate** — the ligand binds through two donor atoms at once, forming a chelate ring. Examples: ethane-1,2-diamine \(\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2\) (en), which binds through its two nitrogen atoms, and the oxalate ion \(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}\), which binds through two oxygen atoms.

**Ambidentate** — a unidentate ligand that contains two different donor atoms and can attach through either one, though only one at a time. Examples: the nitrite ion \(\text{NO}_2^{-}\), which binds through nitrogen as \(-\text{NO}_2\) (nitrito-N) or through oxygen as \(-\text{ONO}\) (nitrito-O), and the thiocyanate ion \(\text{SCN}^{-}\), which binds through sulphur as \(-\text{SCN}\) (thiocyanato) or through nitrogen as \(-\text{NCS}\) (isothiocyanato).

Let the oxidation number of the metal be \(x\) and set the sum of the metal and ligand charges equal to the charge on the entity. Neutral ligands (\(\text{H}_2\text{O}\), en, \(\text{NH}_3\)) contribute zero.

(i) \([\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})(\text{CN})(\text{en})_2]^{2+}\): one \(\text{CN}^{-}\) contributes \(-1\), so \(x - 1 = +2\), giving \(x = +3\).

(ii) \([\text{CoBr}_2(\text{en})_2]^{+}\): two \(\text{Br}^{-}\) contribute \(-2\), so \(x - 2 = +1\), giving \(x = +3\).

(iii) \([\text{PtCl}_4]^{2-}\): four \(\text{Cl}^{-}\) contribute \(-4\), so \(x - 4 = -2\), giving \(x = +2\).

(iv) \(\text{K}_3[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]\): the three \(\text{K}^{+}\) make the complex ion \(3-\), and six \(\text{CN}^{-}\) contribute \(-6\), so \(x - 6 = -3\), giving \(x = +3\).

(v) \([\text{Cr}(\text{NH}_3)_3\text{Cl}_3]\): the entity is neutral and three \(\text{Cl}^{-}\) contribute \(-3\), so \(x - 3 = 0\), giving \(x = +3\).

Oxidation numbers: (i) Co \(+3\), (ii) Co \(+3\), (iii) Pt \(+2\), (iv) Fe \(+3\), (v) Cr \(+3\).

Read the oxidation number from the Roman numeral, add the ligand charges, and supply counter ions to make the whole formula neutral.

(i) Tetrahydroxidozincate(II): \(2 - 4 = -2\), so \([\text{Zn}(\text{OH})_4]^{2-}\)

(ii) Potassium tetrachloridopalladate(II): \(2 - 4 = -2\), so \(\text{K}_2[\text{PdCl}_4]\)

(iii) Diamminedichloridoplatinum(II): \(2 - 2 = 0\), so \([\text{Pt}(\text{NH}_3)_2\text{Cl}_2]\)

(iv) Potassium tetracyanidonickelate(II): \(2 - 4 = -2\), so \(\text{K}_2[\text{Ni}(\text{CN})_4]\)

(v) Pentaamminenitrito-O-cobalt(III): the nitrite is bound through oxygen, \(3 - 1 = +2\), so \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5(\text{ONO})]^{2+}\)

(vi) Hexaamminecobalt(III) sulphate: the cation is \(3+\) and sulphate is \(2-\), so \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]_2(\text{SO}_4)_3\)

(vii) Potassium tri(oxalato)chromate(III): \(3 - 6 = -3\), so \(\text{K}_3[\text{Cr}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]\)

(viii) Hexaammineplatinum(IV): all ligands neutral, so \([\text{Pt}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{4+}\)

(ix) Tetrabromidocuprate(II): \(2 - 4 = -2\), so \([\text{CuBr}_4]^{2-}\)

(x) Pentaamminenitrito-N-cobalt(III): the nitrite is bound through nitrogen, \(3 - 1 = +2\), so \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5(\text{NO}_2)]^{2+}\)

Name the ligands in alphabetical order, then the metal with its oxidation number in Roman numerals in brackets; an anionic complex takes the '-ate' suffix on the metal.

(i) \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]\text{Cl}_3\), Co is \(+3\): hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride

(ii) \([\text{Pt}(\text{NH}_3)_2\text{Cl}(\text{NH}_2\text{CH}_3)]\text{Cl}\), Pt is \(+2\): diamminechlorido(methanamine)platinum(II) chloride

(iii) \([\text{Ti}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}\), Ti is \(+3\): hexaaquatitanium(III) ion

(iv) \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_4\text{Cl}(\text{NO}_2)]\text{Cl}\), Co is \(+3\): tetraamminechloridonitrito-N-cobalt(III) chloride

(v) \([\text{Mn}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}\), Mn is \(+2\): hexaaquamanganese(II) ion

(vi) \([\text{NiCl}_4]^{2-}\), Ni is \(+2\): tetrachloridonickelate(II) ion

(vii) \([\text{Ni}(\text{NH}_3)_6]\text{Cl}_2\), Ni is \(+2\): hexaamminenickel(II) chloride

(viii) \([\text{Co}(\text{en})_3]^{3+}\), Co is \(+3\): tris(ethane-1,2-diamine)cobalt(III) ion

(ix) \([\text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4]\), Ni is \(0\): tetracarbonylnickel(0)

Coordination compounds show two principal classes of isomerism.

**A. Stereoisomerism** — same bonds, different spatial arrangement.

1. Geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism: the ligands may sit adjacent or opposite. Example: cis- and trans-\([\text{Pt}(\text{NH}_3)_2\text{Cl}_2]\).

2. Optical isomerism: mirror images that cannot be superimposed. Example: the d and l forms of \([\text{Co}(\text{en})_3]^{3+}\).

**B. Structural isomerism** — different bonds altogether.

1. Linkage isomerism: an ambidentate ligand binds through a different donor atom. Example: \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5(\text{NO}_2)]\text{Cl}_2\) and \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5(\text{ONO})]\text{Cl}_2\).

2. Coordination isomerism: ligands are interchanged between the cationic and the anionic complex. Example: \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6][\text{Cr}(\text{CN})_6]\) and \([\text{Cr}(\text{NH}_3)_6][\text{Co}(\text{CN})_6]\).

3. Ionisation isomerism: the counter ion and a ligand exchange places. Example: \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5(\text{SO}_4)]\text{Br}\) and \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Br}]\text{SO}_4\).

4. Solvate (hydrate) isomerism: a solvent molecule is inside the coordination sphere in one isomer and merely in the lattice in the other. Example: \([\text{Cr}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]\text{Cl}_3\) (violet) and \([\text{Cr}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_5\text{Cl}]\text{Cl}_2\cdot\text{H}_2\text{O}\) (grey-green).

(i) \([\text{Cr}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]^{3-}\) is of the type \([\text{M(AA)}_3]\): three identical didentate oxalate ligands, each of which can only span a cis edge of the octahedron. Every way of placing them gives the same geometrical arrangement, so **no geometrical isomers are possible** (the number is zero). The entity is nevertheless chiral and exists as a pair of optical isomers.

(ii) \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_3\text{Cl}_3]\) is of the type \(\text{Ma}_3\text{b}_3\). The three like ligands may occupy either three corners of one triangular face of the octahedron, giving the facial (fac) isomer, or three positions around a meridian, giving the meridional (mer) isomer. So **two geometrical isomers are possible**, fac and mer.

Answer: (i) none, (ii) two — the fac and mer isomers.

An octahedral entity is optically active when it has no plane of symmetry, so its mirror image cannot be superimposed on it. Each of these gives a pair of enantiomers, labelled d (dextro) and l (laevo).

(i) \([\text{Cr}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]^{3-}\): the three didentate oxalate ligands wrap round the chromium as a three-bladed propeller. The propeller can twist either way, giving two non-superimposable mirror images — the d and l forms. There is no plane of symmetry, so the whole entity is optically active.

(ii) \([\text{PtCl}_2(\text{en})_2]^{2+}\): only the cis isomer is chiral. In cis-\([\text{PtCl}_2(\text{en})_2]^{2+}\) the two chlorides are adjacent and the two en rings are skewed, so the mirror image is not superimposable and d and l forms exist. The trans isomer has a plane of symmetry and is optically inactive.

(iii) \([\text{Cr}(\text{NH}_3)_2\text{Cl}_2(\text{en})]^{+}\): again only the cis form — with both ammine ligands cis and both chlorido ligands cis — lacks a plane of symmetry, so it exists as a d, l pair. The forms in which either pair is trans have a plane of symmetry and are optically inactive.

Take the geometrical isomers first, then test each for chirality; a didentate en ligand can only span a cis edge.

(i) \([\text{CoCl}_2(\text{en})_2]^{+}\): the two chlorides may be cis or trans, so there are two geometrical isomers. The trans isomer has a plane of symmetry and is optically inactive. The cis isomer has none and exists as a d, l pair. **Total: 3 isomers** — trans, d-cis and l-cis.

(ii) \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)\text{Cl}(\text{en})_2]^{2+}\): the ammine and the chlorido ligand occupy the two sites not taken by the en rings, and they may be cis or trans to each other, giving two geometrical isomers. The trans form is achiral; the cis form is chiral and gives a d, l pair. **Total: 3 isomers**.

(iii) \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_2\text{Cl}_2(\text{en})]^{+}\): the en ring occupies one cis edge and the two ammine and two chlorido ligands share the remaining four sites. There are three geometrical arrangements — the two chlorides trans (ammines cis), the two ammines trans (chlorides cis), and both pairs cis. The first two each possess a plane of symmetry and are optically inactive. The all-cis form has no plane of symmetry and exists as a d, l pair. **Total: 4 isomers** — two achiral geometrical isomers plus one enantiomeric pair.

\([\text{Pt}(\text{NH}_3)(\text{Br})(\text{Cl})(\text{py})]\) is a square planar platinum(II) entity of the type MABCD — four different unidentate ligands.

In a square planar arrangement an isomer is fixed by stating which ligand lies trans to a chosen reference ligand. Taking \(\text{NH}_3\) as the reference, each of the other three ligands in turn can occupy the position trans to it, and the remaining two then fill the other pair of trans sites. That gives **three geometrical isomers**:

1. \(\text{NH}_3\) trans to \(\text{Br}^{-}\) (with \(\text{Cl}^{-}\) trans to py)

2. \(\text{NH}_3\) trans to \(\text{Cl}^{-}\) (with \(\text{Br}^{-}\) trans to py)

3. \(\text{NH}_3\) trans to py (with \(\text{Br}^{-}\) trans to \(\text{Cl}^{-}\))

**None of them exhibits optical isomerism.** All four ligands and the metal lie in one plane, and that molecular plane is itself a plane of symmetry, so each isomer is superimposable on its mirror image.

Answer: three geometrical isomers, none optically active.

In aqueous solution copper sulphate exists as the aqua complex \([\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_4]^{2+}\), and the \(d\)–\(d\) transition of this ion absorbs in the red region, so the solution transmits blue. Adding another ligand in excess replaces the water and changes the crystal field, and hence the colour.

(i) With aqueous potassium fluoride the water ligands are displaced by fluoride:

\([\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_4]^{2+} + 4\text{F}^{-} \rightarrow [\text{CuF}_4]^{2-} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

The potassium salt of this new entity, \(\text{K}_2[\text{CuF}_4]\), is sparingly soluble and separates as the **green precipitate**.

(ii) With aqueous potassium chloride the water is displaced by chloride:

\([\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_4]^{2+} + 4\text{Cl}^{-} \rightarrow [\text{CuCl}_4]^{2-} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

\(\text{K}_2[\text{CuCl}_4]\) is soluble, so the product stays in solution and gives the **bright green solution**.

The colour change in both cases follows from crystal field theory: \(\text{F}^{-}\) and \(\text{Cl}^{-}\) lie below \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) in the spectrochemical series, so replacing water by either of them lowers \(\Delta\). The \(d\)–\(d\) transition therefore requires less energy, the complex absorbs at a longer wavelength than the aqua ion did, and a different complementary colour — green rather than blue — is transmitted.

[Textbook note — the printed key writes the product as \([\text{Cu}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}\), keeping copper at \(+2\). Cyanide is not only a strong-field ligand toward \(\text{Cu(II)}\) but also a reducing agent: it reduces \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) to \(\text{Cu}^{+}\) with evolution of cyanogen, so the species actually isolated is the copper(I) complex \([\text{Cu}(\text{CN})_4]^{3-}\), tetracyanidocuprate(I) — tetracyanidocuprate(II) is not a stable entity in aqueous solution. The answer below therefore names the copper(I) complex. The key's CONCLUSION is unaffected and correct: the complex is so stable that the free \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) concentration stays below the level needed to exceed the solubility product of \(\text{CuS}\), so no precipitate forms with \(\text{H}_2\text{S}\). An examiner following the book will expect the \(2-\) charge, which is why both are named here.] Cyanide is both a strong ligand and a reducing agent, so with excess \(\text{KCN}\) the copper(II) is first reduced to copper(I) and then complexed:

\(2\text{Cu}^{2+} + 10\text{CN}^{-} \rightarrow 2[\text{Cu}(\text{CN})_4]^{3-} + \text{C}_2\text{N}_2\)

The coordination entity formed is therefore \([\text{Cu}(\text{CN})_4]^{3-}\), the tetracyanidocuprate(I) ion, isolated as \(\text{K}_3[\text{Cu}(\text{CN})_4]\).

No precipitate of copper sulphide appears when \(\text{H}_2\text{S}\) is passed through this solution because \([\text{Cu}(\text{CN})_4]^{3-}\) is an extremely stable complex — its stability constant is very large, so it dissociates to give free copper ions only to a negligible extent:

\([\text{Cu}(\text{CN})_4]^{3-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Cu}^{+} + 4\text{CN}^{-}\)

The concentration of free copper ion in solution is consequently so small that the ionic product of copper sulphide never exceeds its solubility product, and precipitation cannot occur.

In each case find the oxidation state, write the \(d\) configuration of the metal ion, then decide from the ligand's field strength whether the electrons pair up (inner orbital, \(d^2sp^3\)) or not (outer orbital, \(sp^3d^2\)).

(i) \([\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]^{4-}\): \(x - 6 = -4\) gives Fe \(+2\), so \(3d^6\). \(\text{CN}^{-}\) is a strong field ligand, so all six electrons pair into three \(3d\) orbitals, leaving two \(3d\) orbitals vacant. Hybridisation \(d^2sp^3\), octahedral, inner orbital (low spin), no unpaired electrons, diamagnetic, \(\mu = 0\,\text{BM}\).

(ii) \([\text{FeF}_6]^{3-}\): \(x - 6 = -3\) gives Fe \(+3\), so \(3d^5\). \(\text{F}^{-}\) is a weak field ligand and causes no pairing, so all five electrons remain unpaired and no \(3d\) orbital is freed. Hybridisation \(sp^3d^2\) using the outer \(4d\) orbitals, octahedral, outer orbital (high spin), five unpaired electrons, \(\mu = \sqrt{35} = 5.92\,\text{BM}\).

(iii) \([\text{Co}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]^{3-}\): \(x - 6 = -3\) gives Co \(+3\), so \(3d^6\). Oxalate is a didentate ligand strong enough to bring about pairing, so the six electrons fill three \(3d\) orbitals and two are left vacant. Hybridisation \(d^2sp^3\), octahedral, inner orbital, no unpaired electrons, diamagnetic, \(\mu = 0\,\text{BM}\).

(iv) \([\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}\): \(x - 6 = -3\) gives Co \(+3\), so \(3d^6\). \(\text{F}^{-}\) is a weak field ligand, so there is no pairing beyond the one pair already present and four electrons stay unpaired. Hybridisation \(sp^3d^2\), octahedral, outer orbital (high spin), four unpaired electrons, \(\mu = \sqrt{24} = 4.90\,\text{BM}\).

The figure is an energy-level diagram drawn in three stages, from left to right.

**Stage 1 — free ion.** The five \(d\) orbitals of the isolated gaseous metal ion are degenerate, drawn as a single level.

**Stage 2 — spherical field.** A hypothetical spherically symmetrical field of the six ligand charges raises all five orbitals together to a higher energy. They remain degenerate; this level is the barycentre.

**Stage 3 — octahedral field.** The real ligands approach along the \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) axes, so the field is asymmetric and the degeneracy is lifted into two sets:

- the lower \(t_{2g}\) set — \(d_{xy}\), \(d_{yz}\), \(d_{zx}\) — drawn as three lines below the barycentre. These orbitals point between the axes, away from the ligands, so they are less repelled and are stabilised by \(0.4\Delta_o\).

- the upper \(e_g\) set — \(d_{x^2-y^2}\), \(d_{z^2}\) — drawn as two lines above the barycentre. These orbitals point along the axes, straight at the ligands, so they are more repelled and are destabilised by \(0.6\Delta_o\).

The vertical gap between the two sets is labelled \(\Delta_o\), the crystal field splitting energy for an octahedral field. Because \(3 \times 0.4\Delta_o = 2 \times 0.6\Delta_o\), the total energy is unchanged relative to the barycentre.

The **spectrochemical series** is the arrangement of ligands in order of the crystal field splitting energy they produce, that is in order of increasing \(\Delta_o\). It is obtained experimentally from the absorption spectra of complexes:

\(\text{I}^{-} < \text{Br}^{-} < \text{SCN}^{-} < \text{Cl}^{-} < \text{S}^{2-} < \text{F}^{-} < \text{OH}^{-} < \text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} < \text{H}_2\text{O} < \text{NCS}^{-} < \text{edta}^{4-} < \text{NH}_3 < \text{en} < \text{CN}^{-} < \text{CO}\)

The difference between the two kinds of ligand is a comparison of \(\Delta_o\) with the pairing energy \(P\).

A **weak field ligand** produces a small splitting, \(\Delta_o < P\). It costs less energy to promote an electron into the upper \(e_g\) set than to pair it in the lower \(t_{2g}\) set, so the electrons stay unpaired as far as possible. The result is a high spin complex with the maximum number of unpaired electrons — strongly paramagnetic. Examples: \(\text{I}^{-}\), \(\text{F}^{-}\), \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\).

A **strong field ligand** produces a large splitting, \(\Delta_o > P\). Pairing now costs less than promotion, so the electrons fill the \(t_{2g}\) set completely before entering \(e_g\). The result is a low spin complex with fewer unpaired electrons. Examples: \(\text{CN}^{-}\), \(\text{CO}\), \(\text{NH}_3\).

**Crystal field splitting energy** is the energy difference between the two sets of \(d\) orbitals produced when the degeneracy of the five \(d\) orbitals is lifted by the field of the ligands. In an octahedral entity the \(d\) orbitals split into the lower \(t_{2g}\) set and the upper \(e_g\) set, and the gap between them is denoted \(\Delta_o\). Its magnitude depends on the field strength of the ligand and on the metal ion.

How \(\Delta_o\) decides the configuration: an electron entering the metal after the \(t_{2g}\) set holds three electrons has two choices. It can go into the upper \(e_g\) set, which costs \(\Delta_o\), or it can pair with an electron already in \(t_{2g}\), which costs the pairing energy \(P\). The system takes the cheaper route.

If \(\Delta_o < P\) (weak field ligand), promotion is cheaper, so the fourth electron enters \(e_g\) and the configuration is \(t_{2g}^3 e_g^1\) — a **high spin** arrangement with the maximum number of unpaired electrons.

If \(\Delta_o > P\) (strong field ligand), pairing is cheaper, so the fourth electron pairs in \(t_{2g}\) and the configuration is \(t_{2g}^4 e_g^0\) — a **low spin** arrangement with fewer unpaired electrons.

So it is the magnitude of \(\Delta_o\) relative to \(P\) that fixes the actual \(d\)-orbital configuration, and with it the magnetic behaviour of the entity.

\([\text{Cr}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{3+}\): the charge balance \(x = +3\) makes the ion \(\text{Cr}^{3+}\), which is \(3d^3\). In the octahedral field the three electrons occupy the three separate \(t_{2g}\) orbitals singly, following Hund's rule — \(t_{2g}^3 e_g^0\). No pairing is possible with only three electrons in three degenerate orbitals, so the strength of the ligand makes no difference here: three unpaired electrons always remain, and the ion is **paramagnetic**, with

\(\mu = \sqrt{3(3+2)} = \sqrt{15} = 3.87\,\text{BM}\)

\([\text{Ni}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}\): the charge balance \(x - 4 = -2\) makes the ion \(\text{Ni}^{2+}\), which is \(3d^8\) with two unpaired electrons in the free ion. \(\text{CN}^{-}\) is a strong field ligand, so those two electrons are forced to pair, and this vacates one \(3d\) orbital. That orbital hybridises with the \(4s\) and two \(4p\) orbitals to give \(dsp^2\), so the ion is square planar. Every \(d\) electron is now paired, so there are no unpaired electrons and the ion is **diamagnetic**, \(\mu = 0\,\text{BM}\).

The colour of a coordination compound arises from a \(d\)–\(d\) transition, in which an electron in the lower set of \(d\) orbitals absorbs visible light and is promoted to the upper set. For that to happen the complex must have a partly filled lower set and a vacancy above it, and the energy gap must lie in the visible range.

\([\text{Ni}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}\): \(\text{Ni}^{2+}\) is \(3d^8\) and \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) is a weak field ligand, so \(\Delta_o\) is small and the octahedral \(t_{2g}^6 e_g^2\) arrangement leaves the \(e_g\) set only partly filled. A \(d\)–\(d\) transition of low energy is therefore possible; the ion absorbs in the red region of the visible spectrum and transmits the complementary colour, so the solution looks **green**.

\([\text{Ni}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}\): \(\text{CN}^{-}\) is a strong field ligand. It pairs up the two unpaired \(3d\) electrons of \(\text{Ni}^{2+}\), giving a square planar \(dsp^2\) ion in which all eight \(d\) electrons are paired in four orbitals. The splitting produced by \(\text{CN}^{-}\) is very large, so the only available transition needs far more energy than visible light can supply — the absorption falls in the ultraviolet. No visible light is absorbed, and the solution is therefore **colourless**.

In both ions iron is in the \(+2\) state, so the metal ion is the same, \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) \((3d^6)\). The colour of each comes from a \(d\)–\(d\) transition in which an electron is promoted from the \(t_{2g}\) set to the \(e_g\) set, and the energy of that transition is exactly the crystal field splitting \(\Delta_o\).

\(\Delta_o\) depends on the ligand. In the spectrochemical series \(\text{CN}^{-}\) lies far above \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\), so

\(\Delta_o[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]^{4-} > \Delta_o[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}\)

Since \(E = hc/\lambda\), the larger splitting in the cyanido complex means it absorbs light of shorter wavelength, while the aqua complex absorbs at longer wavelength. Each transmits the colour complementary to what it absorbs, and because the two absorb at different wavelengths the two solutions show different colours.

The metal–carbon bond in a metal carbonyl has both \(\sigma\) and \(\pi\) character, and the two components reinforce each other.

**The \(\sigma\) component.** The carbon atom of carbon monoxide carries a lone pair, which it donates into a vacant hybrid orbital of the metal. This is a ligand-to-metal \(\sigma\) donation, \(\text{OC} \rightarrow \text{M}\).

**The \(\pi\) component.** A filled \(d\) orbital of the metal overlaps with a vacant antibonding \(\pi^{*}\) orbital of the carbon monoxide, so electron density flows back the other way. This is metal-to-ligand \(\pi\) back-bonding, \(\text{M} \rightarrow \text{CO}\).

**Synergic effect.** The two act together. The \(\sigma\) donation builds up negative charge on the metal, which strengthens the back-donation; the back-donation removes that excess charge, which in turn makes the metal a better acceptor of the \(\sigma\) lone pair. Each strengthens the other, which is why the bonding is called synergic and why metal carbonyls are so stable.

**Consequences.** Back-donation puts electron density into an orbital that is antibonding with respect to C and O, so the metal–carbon bond acquires double bond character and is strengthened, while the carbon–oxygen bond order falls below three and is weakened. This is confirmed experimentally: the C–O stretching frequency in a metal carbonyl is lower than that of free carbon monoxide.

For each complex find the oxidation state from the charge balance, subtract it from the group configuration to get the \(d\) occupation, and count the donor atoms for the coordination number.

(i) \(\text{K}_3[\text{Co}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]\): three \(\text{K}^{+}\) make the anion \(3-\); three oxalate ligands contribute \(-6\), so \(x - 6 = -3\) and cobalt is \(+3\). Configuration \(3d^6\); oxalate is a strong enough field ligand to pair the electrons, so \(t_{2g}^6 e_g^0\). Each oxalate is didentate, so the coordination number is \(3 \times 2 = 6\).

(ii) \(cis\text{-}[\text{CrCl}_2(\text{en})_2]\text{Cl}\): the complex ion is \(1+\) and two chlorido ligands contribute \(-2\), so \(x - 2 = +1\) and chromium is \(+3\). Configuration \(3d^3\), that is \(t_{2g}^3 e_g^0\). Two chlorido donors plus two didentate en ligands give a coordination number of \(2 + 4 = 6\).

(iii) \((\text{NH}_4)_2[\text{CoF}_4]\): two ammonium ions make the anion \(2-\); four fluoride ligands contribute \(-4\), so \(x - 4 = -2\) and cobalt is \(+2\). Configuration \(3d^7\); fluoride is a weak field ligand, so the arrangement is high spin. Coordination number 4.

(iv) \([\text{Mn}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]\text{SO}_4\): sulphate is \(2-\), so the complex ion is \(2+\); water is neutral, so manganese is \(+2\). Configuration \(3d^5\); water is a weak field ligand, so the arrangement is high spin \(t_{2g}^3 e_g^2\). Coordination number 6.

In each case the oxidation state comes from the charge balance, the magnetic moment from the spin only formula \(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\,\text{BM}\) where \(n\) is the number of unpaired electrons.

(i) \(\text{K}[\text{Cr}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_2]\cdot 3\text{H}_2\text{O}\) — potassium diaquadioxalatochromate(III) trihydrate. \(x - 4 = -1\), so Cr is \(+3\); configuration \(3d^3\) \((t_{2g}^3)\); coordination number 6. Octahedral, and since it is of the type \([\text{M(AA)}_2\text{B}_2]\) it shows cis and trans geometrical isomers, the cis form being optically active. Three unpaired electrons, \(\mu = \sqrt{15} = 3.87\,\text{BM}\).

(ii) \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Cl}]\text{Cl}_2\) — pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride. \(x - 1 = +2\), so Co is \(+3\); configuration \(3d^6\), and \(\text{NH}_3\) forces pairing to give \(t_{2g}^6 e_g^0\) \((d^2sp^3\), inner orbital); coordination number 6, octahedral. Being of the type \(\text{Ma}_5\text{b}\) it has no isomers. No unpaired electrons, \(\mu = 0\,\text{BM}\) (diamagnetic).

(iii) \([\text{CrCl}_3(\text{py})_3]\) — trichloridotripyridinechromium(III). The entity is neutral and three chlorides contribute \(-3\), so Cr is \(+3\); configuration \(3d^3\); coordination number 6, octahedral. Being of the type \(\text{Ma}_3\text{b}_3\) it shows facial and meridional geometrical isomers. Three unpaired electrons, \(\mu = \sqrt{15} = 3.87\,\text{BM}\).

(iv) \(\text{Cs}[\text{FeCl}_4]\) — caesium tetrachloridoferrate(III). \(x - 4 = -1\), so Fe is \(+3\); configuration \(3d^5\), and \(\text{Cl}^{-}\) is a weak field ligand so the ion stays high spin; coordination number 4, tetrahedral. Five unpaired electrons, \(\mu = \sqrt{35} = 5.92\,\text{BM}\).

(v) \(\text{K}_4[\text{Mn}(\text{CN})_6]\) — potassium hexacyanidomanganate(II). \(x - 6 = -4\), so Mn is \(+2\); configuration \(3d^5\), and \(\text{CN}^{-}\) is a strong field ligand so the electrons pair to give \(t_{2g}^5 e_g^0\) \((d^2sp^3\), inner orbital); coordination number 6, octahedral. One unpaired electron, \(\mu = \sqrt{3} = 1.73\,\text{BM}\).

In \([\text{Ti}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}\) the charge balance gives titanium the \(+3\) oxidation state, so \(\text{Ti}^{3+}\) has the configuration \(3d^1\) — a single \(d\) electron.

The six water molecules set up an octahedral crystal field, which lifts the degeneracy of the \(d\) orbitals into the lower \(t_{2g}\) set and the upper \(e_g\) set, separated by \(\Delta_o\). In the ground state the one electron occupies a \(t_{2g}\) orbital.

When the complex is placed in visible light, the electron absorbs a photon whose energy matches \(\Delta_o\) and is promoted from \(t_{2g}\) to \(e_g\):

\(t_{2g}^1 e_g^0 \rightarrow t_{2g}^0 e_g^1\)

For the aqua ligand this \(d\)–\(d\) transition corresponds to absorption in the yellow-green region of the spectrum, near \(500\,\text{nm}\). The light that passes through is the remainder of the white light, and the complementary colour of yellow-green is violet. The complex therefore appears **violet**.

The explanation also predicts what happens on heating: if the aqua ligands are driven off, the crystal field and hence the splitting disappear, no \(d\)–\(d\) transition is possible, and the compound becomes colourless.

When a didentate or polydentate ligand attaches itself to the same metal ion through two or more of its donor atoms, it closes a ring with the metal. Such a ring is called a chelate, and the ligand is described as chelating. The **chelate effect** is the observation that a complex formed by a chelating ligand is markedly more stable than a comparable complex formed by the same number of equivalent unidentate donors.

The main reason is entropy. One chelating ligand displaces several unidentate ligands, so the number of free particles in solution increases and the entropy change for the substitution is positive, which makes the free energy change more negative and the complex more stable. Five- and six-membered chelate rings are the most stable, and stability increases with the number of rings formed.

Example: in

\([\text{Ni}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} + 3\,\text{en} \rightarrow [\text{Ni}(\text{en})_3]^{2+} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

three en ligands replace six water molecules and form three five-membered rings. \([\text{Ni}(\text{en})_3]^{2+}\) is far more stable than \([\text{Ni}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{2+}\), even though nickel is bound to six nitrogen donor atoms in both, because only the former is chelated.

(i) **Biological systems.** Many molecules essential to life are coordination compounds of a metal held by a chelating ring. Chlorophyll, the green pigment of plants that carries out photosynthesis, is a coordination compound of magnesium; haemoglobin, the red pigment of blood that transports oxygen, is a coordination compound of iron; and vitamin \(\text{B}_{12}\), cyanocobalamin, is a coordination compound of cobalt.

(ii) **Medicinal chemistry.** *cis*-platin, \(cis\text{-}[\text{Pt}(\text{NH}_3)_2\text{Cl}_2]\), is used to inhibit the growth of tumours. Chelate therapy uses ligands that bind a toxic metal and let it be excreted — EDTA is used to treat lead poisoning, and d-penicillamine and desferrioxime remove excess copper and iron from the body.

(iii) **Analytical chemistry.** EDTA is used in complexometric titration to estimate the hardness of water, since it chelates the \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\) and \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\) present. Nickel is estimated gravimetrically as its bright red complex with dimethylglyoxime, and many metal ions are detected by the characteristic colours of the complexes they form.

(iv) **Extraction and metallurgy of metals.** Silver and gold are extracted from their ores by treatment with cyanide, which dissolves them as the soluble complexes \([\text{Ag}(\text{CN})_2]^{-}\) and \([\text{Au}(\text{CN})_2]^{-}\); the metal is then displaced by adding zinc. Nickel is refined by the Mond process, in which impure nickel is converted to volatile \([\text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4]\) that decomposes on stronger heating to give pure nickel.

The magnetic moment follows the spin only formula \(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\,\text{BM}\), so the ion with the most unpaired electrons has the highest value. All three ligands here are \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\), a weak field ligand, so no pairing beyond that already present in the free ion occurs.

\([\text{Cr}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}\): chromium is \(+3\), so \(\text{Cr}^{3+}\) is \(3d^3\), giving \(n = 3\) and \(\mu = \sqrt{15} = 3.87\,\text{BM}\).

\([\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}\): iron is \(+2\), so \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) is \(3d^6\); high spin \(t_{2g}^4 e_g^2\) leaves \(n = 4\) and \(\mu = \sqrt{24} = 4.90\,\text{BM}\).

\([\text{Zn}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}\): zinc is \(+2\), so \(\text{Zn}^{2+}\) is \(3d^{10}\), completely filled, giving \(n = 0\) and \(\mu = 0\,\text{BM}\).

The highest magnetic moment belongs to the hexaaquairon(II) ion, \([\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}\), at \(4.90\,\text{BM}\).

From the spectrochemical series the field strength increases in the order

\(\text{H}_2\text{O} < \text{NH}_3 < \text{NO}_2^{-}\)

so the splitting increases in the same order:

\(\Delta_o[\text{Ni}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} < \Delta_o[\text{Ni}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{2+} < \Delta_o[\text{Ni}(\text{NO}_2)_6]^{4-}\)

The energy absorbed and the wavelength absorbed are inversely related, \(E = hc/\lambda\), so the larger the splitting the shorter the wavelength absorbed. Reversing the order above gives the order of wavelengths:

\(\lambda[\text{Ni}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} > \lambda[\text{Ni}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{2+} > \lambda[\text{Ni}(\text{NO}_2)_6]^{4-}\)

That is, the hexaaqua ion absorbs at the longest wavelength and the hexanitrito ion at the shortest.
